issues.problem: The demonstration the question asks for is not in the answer's code. Verified replacement code below on sklearn 1.9.1: broken rows identical; predictions [0 0 0 0] broken vs [1 0 1 1] fixed.
issues.replacement:
Demonstration (toy data, only to show the collision):
```python
tx = ["the food was good", "the service was good", "really good value", "not good at all",
      "the room was not good", "good but not clean", "bad and rude", "the food was bad",
      "not bad at all, quite nice", "not bad, enjoyed it", "never disappointing, great",
      "great and not boring"]
y = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]
for w in ["not", "no", "never", "nor", "cannot"]:
    assert w in ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS
v = broken_vec().fit(tx)
print(v.transform(["good", "not good"]).toarray())   # two identical rows
q = ["good", "not good", "bad", "not bad"]
print(fit_predict(broken_vec(), tx, y, q))            # [0 0 0 0]: 'not X' always equals 'X'
print(fit_predict(fixed_vec(), tx, y, q))             # [1 0 1 1]: 'not good' -> 0, 'not bad' -> 1
```
The fixed pipeline separates 'not good' from 'good' and 'not bad' from 'bad', but on this tiny corpus it still labels bare 'bad' positive; the toy data only demonstrates the collision, it is not a quality claim.

reasons: Diagnoses and priorities are sound. The Run C statistical argument conflates sampling uncertainty of the accuracy estimate with epoch-to-epoch variation of one model on a fixed validation set.

issues.claim: With 300 images and accuracy near 70%, the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.7*0.3/300), about 2.6 points, so swings of a few points are expected.
issues.problem: Arithmetic is right (2.6 points) but the binomial SE describes sampling error of the estimate, not changes between epochs on the same 300 images; epoch-to-epoch swings come from the model flipping a handful of predictions (each image is 0.33 points).
issues.replacement: With 300 images and accuracy near 70%, the binomial standard error is sqrt(0.7*0.3/300), about 2.6 points, and each image is worth 0.33 points, so a gap of a few points between epochs is within noise; on a fixed set the swings come from SGD noise flipping a few predictions (learning rate still high, no averaging).

reasons: Degradation problem, gradient argument and shape-mismatch handling are correct (Option A zero-pad / Option B 1x1 projection confirmed in He et al.). Missing conditions: the original ResNet applies ReLU after the addition, and the authors themselves argue degradation is unlikely to be due to vanishing gradients.

issues.claim: This helps gradients reach early layers and eases optimisation, though it does not remove every training difficulty (normalisation, initialisation and learning rate still matter).
issues.problem: The clean identity path holds exactly for pre-activation blocks (original ResNet: 'second nonlinearity after the addition'); the original paper says degradation 'is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients' since the plain nets use batch norm.
issues.replacement: This helps gradients reach early layers and eases optimisation. The identity path is exact in pre-activation blocks; the original ResNet applies a ReLU after the addition. He et al. also argue the degradation is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients (the plain nets use batch norm), so read the identity path as easing optimisation, not only as a vanishing-gradient fix. It does not remove every training difficulty (normalisation, initialisation and learning rate still matter).
